extracted.intended_audience: literate politically-interested readers and policymakers (contemporary to late-18th-century Britain) and modern readers of political criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Normative critique of the National Assembly's constitution, military arrangements, and revenue/finance management during the French Revolution; articulates standards for sound military governance and public finance. Useful as a set of evaluative criteria for assessing revolutionary/state institutions and fiscal policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military command requires personal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The officer in supreme command must be a real, vigorous, effective, decided, personal authority; a king who is not everything in the command of an army is nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘They must be constrained (and their inclinations lead them to what their necessities require) by a real, vigorous, effective, decided, personal authority.’’ The pamphlet argues that nominal heads or divided command reduce obedience and render the supreme commander ineffective; personal authority is essential for delicate military administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer must be first in the soldier's esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: To secure a real army, the officer should be first and last in the eye of the soldier; first and last in his attention, observance, and esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text stresses the cultural and institutional position of officers as the central point of military subordination; weakening that relationship (by elections, faction, or divided patronage) undermines discipline and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing soldiers with municipal clubs and confederacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixing mutinous soldiers with seditious citizens and municipal confederacies will aggravate the confusion from which they have arisen; such schemes weaken military connection and add mutinous audacity to turbulent artisans and peasants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘If the soldiers once come to mix for any time in the municipal clubs, cabals, and confederacies, an elective attraction will draw them to the lowest and most desperate part.’’ The pamphlet treats any prolonged political mingling as a cause of faction and breakdown of military order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double/unclear appointment mechanisms for officers
rubrics_metrics.description: A double negotiation for military rank (e.g., provisional nomination by the king with Assembly approbation) promotes faction and poisons the officer corps; a single clear appointing authority is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘This double negotiation for military rank seems to me a contrivance ... to promote faction in the Assembly itself... and then to poison the corps of officers with factions... destructive in the end to the efficiency of the army itself.’’ The pamphlet warns that divided patronage directs officers' loyalties to factional intrigue rather than command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative oversight must be stable and durable
rubrics_metrics.description: An army will least of all yield obedience to an assembly which is only to have a continuance of two years; transient representative bodies are ill-suited to promote military obedience and discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pamphlet argues that short-term or revolving assemblies create political uncertainty and inconsistent military policy, leaving officers and soldiers without stable authority to respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not encourage soldiers to assert political choice over officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Telling soldiers they are citizens with the rights of man will lead them to exercise a negative in the choice of their officers and to seek elective influence, undermining military subordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘The soldier is told he is a citizen and has the rights of man and citizen... he will exercise at least a negative in the choice of his officers.’’ The pamphlet highlights how political doctrine taught to soldiers converts into demands for electoral control over military appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent emergence of a popular military strongman
rubrics_metrics.description: When officers remain mutinous and factional, some popular general, who understands conciliating the soldiery and possesses the true spirit of command, will arise and command the army—and thereby the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘The moment... that event shall happen, the person who really commands the army is your master... the master of your king, the master of your Assembly, the master of your whole republic.’’ The pamphlet treats the rise of a charismatic military leader as a structural risk of weak civil-military relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the chain of military subordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Destroying the principle of obedience in the critical link between officer and soldier undermines the whole system of military subordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author points to deliberate policies that 'debauch' soldiers from officers (teaching them civic rights etc.) and warns that the central point around which armies are at repose must be maintained to avoid systemic collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal armies must be coherently integrated with the state
rubrics_metrics.description: A municipal army unconnected with the crown or kingdom, though simple in itself, is a monster when considered in relation to the crown, the National Assembly, the public tribunals, or the other army, and can terminate in national calamity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cautions against creating numerous locally controlled military bodies that lack coherence and connection with national institutions; such arrangements are compared unfavorably to ill-devised historical confederations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue is the foundation of the state
rubrics_metrics.description: The revenue of the state is the state; all public virtue and the exercise of public office depend on a just and adequate revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘Through the revenue alone the body politic can act in its true genius and character... the revenue ... becomes in its administration the sphere of every active virtue.’’ The pamphlet makes revenue management central to evaluating government competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of a financier (standards for sound finance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects of a financier are to secure an ample revenue, to impose it with judgment and equality, to employ it economically, and when using credit, to secure its foundations by clearness and candor, exactness of calculations and solidity of funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit checklist used to judge the Assembly's managers: adequacy of revenue, fairness of imposition, economy in expenditure, prudent credit usage, transparency in accounts, and soundness of financial instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not abolish old taxes before providing replacements or compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Declaring old revenue systems oppressive and simultaneously ordering their payment until replacement—which is not provided—leads to provincial resistance and breakdown of revenue collection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pamphlet describes salt-monopoly reforms and the Assembly's failure to provide an equitable replacement or compensation to provinces, provoking noncompliance and fiscal collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on voluntary 'benevolences' as fiscal policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary contributions disguised as 'benevolence' are weak, ineffective, unequal, and a poor response to fiscal necessity—'a tax of regulation upon virtue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer calls such measures 'the rickety offspring of weakness' and argues they cannot reliably fill state needs; when enforced they become coercive and corrosive of legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ad hoc patriotic donations and confiscations as main revenue sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Patriotic donations, the pillaging of crown ornaments and church plate, and coerced gifts are ruinous to trades and public credit and are poor substitutes for systemic revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pamphlet likens these measures to desperate, ill-conceived tricks that ruin commerce and exhaust the willingness of contributors, and warns they cannot be repeated successfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper money must be voluntary in use and convertible; not a substitute for real credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper money is valuable in commerce only if received by choice, originated in cash deposits, and is freely convertible into coin; if not, paper becomes the badge of distress not prosperity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘In England not one shilling of paper money... is received but of choice... it is convertible at pleasure... Our paper is of value in commerce, because in law it is of none.’’ Maintain legal and practical convertibility and sound backing for paper currency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial reform must control public expenditure as well as revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Economies must include scrutiny of new expenses (Assembly, municipalities, armies, police, judicatures, pensions); reducing some prodigal expenses does not compensate for large new outlays—the new system may be more chargeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pamphlet urges comparing present expenses against the shrunken revenues and warns that apparent economies are negated by expanded institutions and obligations created by the new regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central authority must ensure equitable tax distribution and avoid local unilateralism
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing districts to judge which old taxes they may withhold introduces a new and oppressive inequality: the most submissive parts bear the whole burden while others refuse payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author faults the Assembly's tolerance of districts dropping taxes and concludes that without central enforcement or fair replacement, tax equity collapses and fiscal capacity fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy must be consistent with declared principles (avoid hypocritical contradictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching people to abhor feudality and then preserving feudal burdens (rents) without redress is inconsistent and breeds resentment; declared rights must align with practical redress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pamphlet points out the hypocrisy of abolishing titles and honors while keeping the financial burdens linked to feudal origins, and argues for coherent application of principles to outcomes (e.g., rents, succession).
